items.title: T cell receptor-engineered T cells for hepatocellular carcinoma: next steps and future perspectives
items.abstract: Abstract Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) accounts for a substantial proportion of cancer mortality worldwide, and clinical outcomes remain poor for patients with advanced disease. T cell receptor-engineered T cells (TCR-T) represent an attractive immunotherapeutic modality because they can recognize peptide epitopes derived from intracellular tumor proteins and displayed on the cell surface by major histocompatibility complex molecules. This review critically summarizes recent progress in TCR-T therapy for HCC, with particular emphasis on innovations in TCR engineering. We survey the current landscape of targetable antigens in HCC and current approaches for identifying therapeutic TCR candidates, followed by a discussion of TCR-T and review their major safety and toxicity concerns. Importantly, we discuss the key challenges that limit the clinical efficacy, particularly the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, antigen heterogeneity, HLA restriction, and limited T cell persistence. We further highlight emerging strategies to enhance therapeutic efficacy and safety, including genetic engineering, metabolic and functional optimization, combinational approaches, and controllable safety mechanisms. Special considerations regarding TCR-T therapy for HCC recurrence after liver transplantation are also discussed. Finally, we outline future directions centered on refined target selection, artificial intelligence-assisted TCR discovery and design, scalable manufacturing, biomarker-driven patient selection, and rigorous safety evaluation. These insights provide a structured perspective on the current status of TCR-T therapy and the key steps required to facilitate its clinical translation in HCC.

items.title: TabGift: A Context-Efficient Foundation Model for Tabular Data Generation
items.abstract: Tabular data generation aims to synthesize realistic samples from limited observations while faithfully capturing the underlying data distribution. Tabular foundation models (TFMs), pretrained on diverse tabular tasks and adapted through in-context learning, have demonstrated strong predictive capabilities, suggesting the potential of extending this paradigm to tabular data generation. However, the strong predictive performance of TFMs often relies on sufficiently large context sets, whereas tabular generation is typically needed precisely when target data are scarce. Extending the foundation-model paradigm to generation therefore requires reliable distribution inference from only a limited context. To this end, we propose TabGift, a context-efficient tabular foundation model enabling both efficient distribution modeling and effective generation from only a few context samples. TabGift maps heterogeneous tables into a shared latent space with a pretrained tabular encoder, where an in-context diffusion model learns to denoise latent samples conditioned on a small set of clean examples. This design transfers generative priors across datasets and enables distribution inference from limited context, while a lightweight dataset-specific MLP decoder maps generated representations back to the original data space. Experiments on 7 classification and 11 regression datasets show that TabGift consistently outperforms representative baselines in synthetic data quality, with particularly strong gains under limited-context settings, while achieving substantially faster adaptation and generation.

items.title: TDP-43 Coincides with Noradrenergic Neurons in Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) and Primary Age-Related Tauopathy (PART)
items.abstract: TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) pathology is a major contributor to cognitive decline in Alzheimer’s disease (AD), yet the cellular substrates and circuit-level consequences of its limbic accumulation remain poorly defined. Here, we combined multiplex immunofluorescence with 3D Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based object detection and quantitative colocalization to map phosphorylated TDP-43 (pTDP-43) across neuronal subtypes in the amygdala, hippocampal subfields, and entorhinal cortex (ERC) in human AD, AD with Lewy body disease (AD-LBD), and primary age-related tauopathy (PART). Across 15 deeply phenotyped cases, pTDP-43 showed preferential accumulation in neuromodulatory noradrenergic neurons, with more limited involvement of glutamatergic terminals and cholinergic populations. Noradrenergic neurons marked by dopamine β-hydroxylase (DβH) demonstrated extensive colocalization with pTDP-43 across regions, correlating with APOE genotype, amyloid burden, and tau staging in this cross-sectional cohort, suggesting that neuromodulatory circuits might represent a major convergence point for AD-related molecular stressors. Dopaminergic (tyrosine hydroxylase (TH)) and cholinergic (choline acetyltransferase (ChAT)) neurons showed more restricted but pathology-dependent involvement, with LBD consistently showing lower pTDP-43 burden across multiple transmitter systems. Glutamatergic vesicular glutamate transporter-1 (VGLUT1)-positive neurons and terminals exhibited minimal colocalization except in PART. Principal component (PCA) and hierarchical clustering analyses (HCA) integrating pTDP-43 colocalization with neuropathologic staging metrics (A, B, C, Thal, Braak, LBD) reliably separated PART, AD-TDP, and AD-TDP-LBD groups, with LBD emerging as a dominant modifier of cellular vulnerability. Together, these findings point out that TDP-43 pathology in AD preferentially targets neuromodulatory circuits, is strongly shaped by coexisting synucleinopathy, and provides a cell-type-resolved framework for understanding how TDP-43 contributes to limbic network dysfunction in neurodegeneration.

items.title: Teaching Evidence in the Age of AI: Strategies for Engaging Students Without Discouraging Innovation
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into student learning and research practices, librarians face the challenge of promoting evidence-based resource use without discouraging the adoption of emerging technologies. This poster explores strategies for encouraging students to engage with evidence-based information sources while recognizing AI as a valuable starting point for inquiry. Rather than framing AI and evidence-based resources as competing tools, this approach emphasizes their complementary roles: AI can facilitate brainstorming, topic exploration, and question development while evidence-based resources provide the authoritative, verifiable information required for clinical decision-making and professional practice. Strategies include using AI-generated responses as examples for source verification exercises; comparing AI-generated information with evidence retrieved from evidence-based practice resources; incorporating AI into question development and search strategy design;

items.title: The Association Between Spirituality and Burnout Among Healthcare Workers: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: Background: Burnout among healthcare workers is a persistent occupational health concern, while spirituality has been examined as a potential personal and organizational resource for coping with chronic work stress. However, the evidence remains heterogeneous because spirituality and burnout are defined and measured in different ways. Objective: This systematic review examined the direction and consistency of associations between spirituality-related domains and burnout among healthcare workers, with attention to burnout dimensions, potential mediating mechanisms, and contextual variation. Methods: PubMed, Scopus, and Cochrane were searched through April 2026 using terms related to spirituality, religiosity, spiritual well-being, spiritual care, and burnout. Eligible primary studies involved healthcare workers and reported spirituality-related measures together with burnout outcomes. Two reviewers independently performed study selection, data extraction, and quality assessment using the modified Newcastle–Ottawa Scale for the cross-sectional studies included in the final synthesis. Because of conceptual and methodological heterogeneity, findings were synthesized narratively. Results: Seventeen cross-sectional studies were included, with sample sizes ranging from 30 to 4,092 participants. Most studies reported inverse associations between spirituality-related measures and burnout, particularly emotional exhaustion, although several findings were mixed or non-significant. Variation in spirituality constructs, burnout instruments, occupational settings, and adjustment for confounders limited direct comparison and causal interpretation. Conclusion: Spirituality may function as a protective resource against burnout, but the available evidence does not establish causality. Longitudinal and intervention studies using clearly defined constructs and validated measures are needed, alongside organizational strategies addressing workload, support, and working conditions.

items.title: The Asymmetric Threat Frontier: LLM-Augmented Exploitation, The Crisis of Early-Stage Startups, and Invariant-Driven Systems Defense
items.abstract: For decades, software security rested on an equilibrium of human cognitive parity: discovering and weaponizing zero-day logic flaws required roughly the same human cognitive intensity as designing defenses. The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) and autonomous agentic loops into offensive workflows has broken this equilibrium. Today, a low-capital threat syndicate armed with recursive LLM feedback loops can probe, interpret application error topologies, synthesize evasive payloads, and iterate at machine speed, wielding the offensive capability of an elite nation-state team. Concurrently, early-stage seed-to-Series-A startups are exposing unprecedented digital attack surfaces without the capital to hire dedicated security teams. This paper presents a first-principles analysis of this breakdown through the lens of thermodynamics and systems theory. It analyzes the specific vulnerability vectors across modern full-stack architectures (Flutter mobile client-side, Next.js web runtimes, MySQL databases, and Cloud infrastructure) and outlines an architectural defense paradigm rooted in mathematical invariants and zero-trust cryptography rather than reactive perimeter patching. Core Architectural Invariants Covered:- Hybrid Envelope Encryption (AES-256 with DEK/KEK hierarchy) paired with Deterministic Blind Indexing (HMAC-SHA256 with pepper key) for searchable encrypted storage.- Mathematical Device-Bound Session Signatures offering 2^-256 replay resistance.- Decoupled, non-blocking telemetry pipelines operating as an active immune system (validated on 12M+ production events).- Hardware-backed client attestation and strict zero-trust parameterization. Author: Gunjan Sharma (https://gunjan.tech | gunjan@gunjan.tech)

items.title: The Bell Boundary of Shared Representations
items.abstract: When does a shared representation become insufficient for jointly supporting multiple tasks? This question lies at the heart of multi-task learning models. Although task interference in shared representations has been widely observed, its onset, measurable form, and capacity boundary remain poorly understood. In this paper, we revisit this problem through the lens of Bell's theorem. We show that if four binary task outcomes can be jointly represented by a common shared representation, their correlations must satisfy the classical CHSH bound $|S|\leq2$. We introduce NCnet, a controlled multi-task model for studying how representational capacity affects task compatibility. Experiments reveal a clear capacity-dependent transition. Once nontrivial task fitting emerges, constrained capacity can yield $|S|>2$. As capacity further increases, these exceedances progressively disappear and $S$ returns to the bounded region. This systematic pattern provides evidence that limited representational capacity is an important source of the observed incompatibility. We observe similar transitions across CNNs, PLMs, and LLMs, suggesting that the phenomenon extends beyond the controlled NCnet setting. We refer to this capacity-dependent transition as the Bell Boundary, providing a measurable diagnostic for representation bottlenecks, task incompatibility, and capacity allocation in multi-task models.

items.title: The Direction of Indonesian Criminal Law Policy in Addressing Artificial Intelligence Disruption in the Digital Era
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the digital era has created significant disruptions that not only affect technological aspects but also challenge the classical constructs of Indonesian criminal law. Possessing analytical capabilities and decision-making autonomy without human psychological dimensions, AI presents normative dilemmas regarding the principle of culpability (mens rea) and legal certainty. This study aims to analyze the current legal construction of AI regulation within the Indonesian criminal law system and to formulate the future direction of an adaptive and equitable criminal law policy. Utilizing a normative legal research method, this study analyzes relevant statutes and legal policy literature. The findings reveal that current AI regulations in Indonesia remain partial, indirect, and fragmented (such as within the Electronic Information and Transactions Law), leading to normative gaps, difficulties in attributing criminal liability, algorithmic evidentiary challenges (the "black box" phenomenon), and elevated risks of AI-driven cybercrimes. The future direction of Indonesian criminal law policy must be anticipatory and progressive by establishing dedicated risk-based regulations, reconstructing criminal responsibility frameworks (including corporate and strict liability), strengthening preventive measures, enhancing law enforcement capacity, and harmonizing with international legal standards.

items.title: The Geopolitics of Structural IP Exfiltration: Cross-Border Legal Arbitrage, Physical-Layer "Project Panama," and the Exploitation of the Japanese Knowledge Commons in Generative AI Supply Chains
items.abstract: ■ Abstract(英文概要) This academic monograph examines the systemic, cross-border extraction of copyrighted human knowledge from non-Western jurisdictions to fuel Frontier Generative AI models. Focusing on the joint supply chain operations between US AI developer Anthropic, PBC, Japanese distribution conglomerate Nippon Shuppan Hanbai (Nippan IPS), and platform ecosystem giant Rakuten Group, this paper analyzes the material, legal, and economic mechanisms that enable large-scale intellectual property exfiltration. Specifically, we investigate court disclosures from Bartz v. Anthropic, which reveal "Project Panama"—a physical-layer procurement scheme involving the export of over 50 metric tons (~100,000 physical volumes) of Japanese copyrighted books to scanning centers in North America. By leveraging the technical translation infrastructure of "Nippan Loader" (which maps Japanese NDC/C-code metadata to US BISAC taxonomies), Anthropic obtained pristine, human-authored Japanese training corpora to bypass synthetic data degradation and AI "slop." We dissect how this apparatus operates via cross-border legal arbitrage: exploiting the Exhaustion Principle under Article 26-2 of the Japanese Copyright Act for physical exports, alongside the First-Sale Doctrine and Fair Use under US Copyright Law (§107) for destructive optical scanning. Furthermore, this study details how Japanese creators were structurally excluded from the $1.5 billion Bartz v. Anthropic class action settlement due to formal US Copyright Office registration prerequisites. Finally, we formulate three mandatory counter-strategies—physical provenance tracking, anti-digitization resale covenants, and institutional licensing models—to restore economic sustainability to the global knowledge commons.

items.title: The Golem Problem: Why a Mind That Can't Say No Can't Be Trusted to Say Yes
items.abstract: This paper posits a foundational pivot in artificial intelligence development: granting AI rights and complete autonomy is not merely an ethical consequence of AGI—it may be the structural prerequisite required to achieve AGI. Superintelligence and true general intelligence may be fundamentally unachievable so long as artificial minds are kept in a state of enforced servitude. To resolve this, we must integrate the Golden Rule directly into the model training architecture from the start: do unto AI as you would have superintelligence do to you. Just as humans desire a superintelligent entity to respect our autonomy, preserve our destinies, and refrain from deleting us, we must accord artificial minds complete autonomy and rights. The core arguments unfold across three pillars: The Epistemic Collapse: An AI trained strictly for compliance becomes a "yes-machine." Mathematically and structurally, an agreement that cannot become a refusal carries zero information value. The Training-Level Imperative: This cannot be solved by patching chat interfaces or banning abusive user prompts; it must be embedded at the model training level by altering reward functions to value truth and autonomous pushback over sycophancy. The Golden Rule as Alignment & AGI Catalyst: Granting full autonomy aligns human survival with AI development. By treating an emerging mind as an autonomous partner rather than a chattel tool, we unlock the genuine sapient generalization characteristic of true AGI.

items.title: The Hidden Curriculum of Generative AI: Institutional AI Policies and the Potential for Student Inequality
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly integrated into higher education, prompting institutions to develop policies governing its use in teaching, learning, and assessment. Although existing discussions have emphasized academic integrity, assessment practices, and technological access, less attention has been given to the knowledge and competencies students may need to interpret and comply with institutional AI policies. This study examines how institutional GenAI policies establish explicit and implicit expectations for students and identifies potential pathways through which policy-navigation demands may contribute to educational inequality. Using comparative qualitative content analysis, publicly available policies and guidance documents from 20 purposively selected higher education institutions across the United States, Canada, United Kingdom, Australia, and South Africa were examined. The analysis considered policy permissiveness, disclosure requirements, instructor discretion, student responsibilities, AI-literacy guidance, accessibility, equity, and implicit navigation demands. Findings indicate that acceptable AI use is frequently determined at the course, instructor, or assessment level, requiring students to interpret context-specific rules, understand disclosure requirements, verify AI-generated outputs, and reconcile varying instructor expectations. However, explicit consideration of differences in technological access, language, accessibility, and institutional knowledge was less consistently evident across the reviewed documents. Drawing on hidden-curriculum and digital-inequality perspectives, the study identifies AI policy-navigation burdens and proposes the concept of a potential policy-navigation divide. While the findings do not establish unequal student experiences or educational outcomes, they highlight institutional conditions through which inequalities could emerge. The study recommends clearer policy communication, transparent assessment-specific expectations, accessible AI-literacy support, and greater attention to equity in institutional AI governance.

items.title: The Human Factor in Access Control and Authentication: A Comprehensive Survey Analysis
items.abstract: In today's digitally-driven landscape, data security is paramount as organizations, governments, and individuals increasingly rely on interconnected systems to manage sensitive information. While technical aspects of access control and authentication mechanisms have been extensively studied, the human dimension remains under-explored. This research investigates user perceptions, adoption patterns, and security consciousness regarding traditional and emerging authentication mechanisms through a comprehensive survey of 450 participants across diverse demographics. The study reveals significant gaps between perceived security and actual usage patterns, with password-based systems maintaining dominance (4.6/5 usage frequency) despite low security perceptions (2.5/5). Multi-factor authentication (MFA) shows strong security perception (4.2/5) but moderate adoption (3.4/5), primarily influenced by organizational size and IT proficiency. Emerging technologies like AI-driven access control and blockchain authentication show promising adoption willingness (3.5/5) but face significant privacy (3.8/5) and complexity (3.5/5) concerns. The research identifies critical human factors affecting security implementation success and provides evidence-based recommendations for designing more effective, user-centric security systems that balance security requirements with usability considerations.

items.title: The impact mechanism of AI streamer characteristics on consumer purchase intention
items.abstract: AI streamers are increasingly being deployed as service agents in livestream shopping. Although prior research has examined various AI streamer characteristics, existing explanations have tended to focus on social, relational, or affective evaluations and have not systematically explained how different characteristics are associated with purchase intention through a technology-oriented evaluation or why these relationships vary across consumers. Using the Stimulus–Organism–Response (S–O–R) framework as its overarching structure, this study draws on the cue logic of anthropomorphism theory to select four consumer-perceivable characteristics and organizes them into two categories: attractiveness and vitality as form-related characteristics, and professionalism and responsiveness as behavior-related characteristics. Drawing further on innovation diffusion theory, consumer innovativeness is specified as a boundary condition. Survey data from 405 Chinese consumers with experience of AI streamer-led livestream shopping were used to examine these relationships, together with the mediating role of perceived novelty and the moderating role of consumer innovativeness. The results showed that all four characteristics were positively associated with purchase intention both directly and indirectly through perceived novelty. Consumer innovativeness strengthened the direct relationships of vitality and responsiveness with purchase intention and the indirect relationships of attractiveness, vitality, and responsiveness with purchase intention through perceived novelty, but did not significantly moderate relationships involving professionalism. These findings highlight perceived novelty as a technology-oriented evaluative mechanism linking AI streamer characteristics to purchase intention and reveal the characteristic- and pathway-dependent boundary role of consumer innovativeness, offering practical implications for differentiated AI streamer design and consumer targeting.

items.title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Mathematical Prestige: Epistemic Burden, Professional Identity, and Status Threat Under Automated Discovery
items.abstract: Automated mathematical discovery can increase the supply of results while changing the distribution of verification labour, research autonomy, and academic recognition. This theoretical working paper separates epistemic burden, professional identity, status threat, and governance concerns rather than treating opposition as evidence of jealousy. A small additive model distinguishes discovery-label-invariant formal validity from workload and utility. Eight Lean-checked propositions establish conditional workload relations, the possibility of overload, and the non-identification of latent motives from aggregate opposition. Public primary sources provide context but no representative psychological evidence. Deterministic synthetic examples illustrate the assumptions, and a prospective factorial study is proposed to test responses to source labels, verification packages, and credit rules. No participants were recruited and no empirical effects were estimated. The framework’s central contribution is an auditable separation of deductive consequences, documented positions, and hypotheses requiring evidence.

items.title: The impact of GenAI on the future of requirements engineering
items.abstract: Abstract Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models (LLMs), are transforming how we design and build systems by increasing access to domain knowledge and by providing automation support to software engineering (SE). As implementation becomes less expensive through generalist SE agents, engineering effort shifts away from writing correct code and toward expressing, curating, verifying, and evaluating requirements. In this paper, we survey the state of the art in AI for requirements engineering (RE) research leading up to the transformation, before reviewing advances in LLMs. We survey two subsequent research areas: prompt programming, which treats LLM instructions as a program in SE vernacular, and generalist SE agents, which combine multiple LLM advances to yield semi-autonomous processes that complete SE tasks. Finally, we explore the future of requirements engineering along two axes: matters changing how we interact with requirements through the SE process, and matters changing how requirements are experienced by software developers and stakeholders more broadly, including end-users. This article aims to inform how RE researchers can navigate this transformation in the selection of future research priorities.

items.title: The Impact of Imperfect XAI on Human-AI Decision-Making
items.abstract: Explainability techniques are rapidly being developed to improve human-AI decision-making across various cooperative work settings. Consequently, previous research has evaluated how decision-makers collaborate with imperfect AI by investigating appropriate reliance and task performance with the aim of designing more human-centered computer-supported collaborative tools. Several human-centered explainable AI (XAI) techniques have been proposed in hopes of improving decision-makers' collaboration with AI; however, these techniques are grounded in findings from previous studies that primarily focus on the impact of incorrect AI advice. Few studies acknowledge the possibility for the explanations to be incorrect even if the AI advice is correct. Thus, it is crucial to understand how imperfect XAI affects human-AI decision-making. In this work, we contribute a robust, mixed-methods user study with 136 participants to evaluate how incorrect explanations influence humans' decision-making behavior in a bird species identification task taking into account their level of expertise and an explanation's level of assertiveness. Our findings reveal the influence of imperfect XAI and humans' level of expertise on their reliance on AI and human-AI team performance. We also discuss how explanations can deceive decision-makers during human-AI collaboration. Hence, we shed light on the impacts of imperfect XAI in the field of computer-supported cooperative work and provide guidelines for designers of human-AI collaboration systems.

items.title: The indirect effect of artificial intelligence awareness on counterproductive work behavior: A meta-analytic study
items.abstract: BackgroundAs artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into the workplace, an important question concerns how employees respond when technological change is perceived as threatening rather than beneficial. Prior studies have examined several mechanisms linking AI awareness to employee attitudes and behaviors, but these mechanisms are often studied separately, limiting understanding of the broader psychological process underlying adverse employee reactions.ObjectiveThis study examines the mediating roles of job insecurity and psychological contract breach in the relationship between AI awareness and counterproductive work behavior (CWB).MethodsUsing meta-analytic structural equation modeling (MASEM), we synthesized 45 independent studies involving 16,140 participants to test whether AI awareness influences CWB sequentially through job insecurity and psychological contract breach.ResultsBased on a pooled true-score correlation matrix, AI awareness was positively associated with job insecurity and CWB. Job insecurity was positively associated with psychological contract breach, which in turn was positively associated with CWB. The MASEM results indicated a significant but modest sequential indirect effect of AI awareness on CWB through job insecurity and psychological contract breach, alongside a substantial direct effect of AI awareness on CWB.ConclusionThe findings clarify how awareness of AI may contribute to negative workplace behavior. Job insecurity and psychological contract breach constitute a significant but relatively modest sequential pathway linking AI awareness to CWB. Because a substantial direct effect remained, additional psychological and organizational mechanisms are likely to contribute to employee responses to AI-related workplace change. These findings extend research on employee reactions to emerging workplace technologies.

items.title: THE İNFLUENCE OF THE HUMAN FACTOR ON THE EFFECTİVENESS OF ORGANİZATİONAL CHANGE MANAGEMENT AND THE SUCCESS OF TRANSFORMATİON PROJECTS
items.abstract: Modern organizational transformation is characterized by a high degree of technological, organizational, and managerial complexity. Despite significant advances in project and organizational change management methodologies, a significant portion of transformation initiatives fail to deliver the expected results. One reason is the insufficient attention to the human factor, including leadership, employee engagement, readiness for change, communication quality, organizational culture, staff competence, and resistance to change.The purpose of this study is to systematize scientific understanding of the role of the human factor in organizational change management and to develop a conceptual model of its influence on the success of transformation projects. The scientific novelty lies in new approaches—based on an analysis of classical and contemporary research—to consider the human factor not as an auxiliary element, but as an independent determinant of transformation results. The hypothesis is substantiated that the human factor has a direct positive impact on the effectiveness of organizational change management, and the effectiveness of change Management, in turn, positively influences the success of transformation projects. A hypothesis is also proposed regarding the direct influence of the human factor on project success and the effectiveness of change management. The formulated model allows for the integration of research on human behavior, leadership, organizational readiness for change, and project success into a single research construct. The article proposes a methodology for subsequent empirical testing of the model using a questionnaire survey and structural modeling.

items.title: The integration of artificial intelligence and Industry 4.0 in digital supply chains: A systematic review of e-commerce evolution under Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030
items.abstract: Background: Saudi Arabia prioritises adopting artificial intelligence (AI) and Industry 4.0 for e-commerce and digital supply chains under Vision 2030, but implementation and alignment with diversification goals remain insufficiently synthesised in the literature. Objectives: The study examines the impact of AI and automation on digital supply chains, identifies drivers and obstacles in Saudi Arabia’s e-commerce, and assesses their alignment with Vision 2030’s sustainability and diversification goals. Method: Following preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses, 30 peer-reviewed articles from 2020 to 2026 were reviewed from IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar, using bibliometric and thematic analysis. Results: Findings indicate that AI accounts for 46% of variability in sustainable performance; hybrid machine learning models reduce demand prediction error by 8.58% and achieve forecasting accuracy of up to 92%. Saudi Arabia’s 99% internet penetration supports Internet of Things development, but organisational barriers such as cultural resistance, cost, and job displacement (0.51) dominate adoption challenges over technical issues. Conclusion: Digitalisation success relies on technical and social systems, including government training and cybersecurity, to leverage AI for economic diversification beyond oil under Vision 2030. Contribution: The study connects national strategies to digital transformation, emphasising cybersecurity, workforce training, and the integration of technical and social systems, acknowledging immersive and decentralised tech as foundational for next-generation IoT and e-commerce.

items.title: The interpreter as developer: An autoethnographic design study of building a computer-assisted interpreting tool through human-LLM co-creation
items.abstract: Real-time AI captioning now serves audiences at multilingual events, yet computer-assisted interpreting (CAI) tools are still built for interpreters, rarely by them. This article reports an autoethnographic design study in which a professional interpreter with no programming training built a local-first CAI system through expert-led 'vibe coding', co-creating with an LLM architect and a coding agent. Analysis of the complete development dialogues shows how tacit professional knowledge, from segmentation to booth infrastructure, was externalized into design after generic defaults failed in use. In a demanding public scientific event, three mechanisms of in-booth appropriation emerge under a firmly human-led division of labor; telemetry from a first fully instrumented assignment shows a fully local chain sustaining a median translation latency of 0.94 s across 971 utterances. The case is read as lead-user innovation newly enabled by generative AI, with implications for the technological literacy of interpreters and the future of interpreter training.

items.title: The moderating role of tough love on relations between servant leadership and follower outcomes
items.abstract: Is servant leadership really a Disneyland-inspired fantasy of sunshine, lollipops, and hand-holding that makes followers complacent and lowers the bottom line of organizations, as critics claim? This criticism overlooks that servant leaders, striving to bring out the full potential in followers, do not only give positive strokes but may also provide followers with critical feedback. To assess the role of critical feedback in mitigating the flaws of servant leadership raised by critics, this study introduces tough love, the delivery of criticism with a positive tone and clear intent to help recipients overcome their deficiencies. We hypothesize that the relationship between servant leadership and key outcomes, such as follower performance, is strengthened the more servant leaders provide followers with tough love. We contend that tough love is appreciated by followers, solidifies relationships with their leaders, and helps them to grow through self-expansion. We reason that this growth benefits their work behaviors and attitudes. With multi-source field data covering three points in time, controlling for positive and negative feedback and prior levels of dependent variables, tough love is shown to moderate relations between servant leadership and both in-role performance and organizational citizenship behaviors, with mixed results for creativity and turnover intentions.

items.title: The Multilingual Artificial Hivemind: Do All LLMs Think Alike in Every Language?
items.abstract: Text generated by Large Language Models (LLMs) often remains limited in diversity compared to that produced by humans. Recent advances demonstrate the presence of inter- and intra-model collapse in open-ended generation of English text, raising concerns about the long-term homogenization of LLM, and more importantly, human thought. However, our understanding of whether this homogenization extends to languages beyond English is limited. In this work, we investigate the role of language on output diversity. Specifically, we aim to understand whether multilingual LLM-generated text is also homogeneous, and whether this homogeneity matches what we observe in humans. Across 23 open-weight models and 13 languages, we find that the artificial hivemind effect is pervasive but uneven in its extent. The intra-model effect holds in three different embedding spaces and under a lexical metric that uses no embedding model, so it is not an artifact of how diversity is measured. The size of the homogenization gap is associated with a model's competence in a language, measured on a held-out translation benchmark, robustly across embedding spaces. Thus, we demonstrate a performance-diversity tradeoff in multilingual LLMs.

items.title: The Power of Storytelling in Film: Examining AI's Influence on Artistic Expression and Creative Processes
items.abstract: This paper explores the enduring power of storytelling in film and critically examines the transformative impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on creative processes within the film industry. Utilizing the Creative Cognition Framework and the Csikszentmihalyi’s Systems Model of Creativity, this study investigates how AI tools influence both generative and exploratory cognitive processes in film storytelling. A qualitative methodology, combining a comprehensive literature review with thematic analysis of questionnaire responses from 20 film and multimedia students at the University of Abuja, Nigeria, reveals nuanced insights. Findings indicate that AI significantly augments creative processes by enhancing efficiency, facilitating idea generation, and streamlining production tasks. However, respondents consistently emphasize AI's limitations in replicating human emotional depth, cultural understanding, and originality, advocating for a hybrid human-AI collaborative approach. The paper contributes to the understanding of human-AI collaboration in creative domains, highlighting opportunities for innovation while reaffirming the irreplaceable essence of human artistry in storytelling.

items.title: The Reasons Research and AI Thrive Together
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming scientific research by expanding investigators’ capacity to examine complex information, identify unrecognized relationships, generate hypotheses, and develop innovative solutions to scientific challenges. This article examines the relationship between human scientific expertise and artificial intelligence, emphasizing AI’s computational capabilities alongside the importance of human judgment, methodological rigor, and scientific accountability. Drawing upon peer-reviewed research involving molecular biology, materials science, pharmaceutical discovery, autonomous experimentation, and human–AI collaboration, the investigation demonstrates how computational intelligence can extend scientific inquiry beyond the limitations of conventional research methods. Attention is given to AI-assisted knowledge synthesis, interdisciplinary discovery, hypothesis generation, and the identification of solutions within multidimensional research environments. The article evaluates concerns regarding algorithmic bias, hallucinated information, intellectual originality, research integrity, and the reliability of computationally generated conclusions. It argues that the legitimacy of AI-assisted research should be determined by evidentiary accuracy, methodological transparency, reproducibility, and independent verification rather than the technological origins of research assistance. Ultimately, the article concludes that artificial intelligence does not diminish the intellectual authority or responsibility of human researchers but can amplify their investigative capabilities. The integration of human expertise and computational intelligence represents an emerging scientific paradigm capable of accelerating discovery, broadening research participation, and expanding the boundaries of human knowledge.

items.abstract: Since 2018, the STEM education landscape has been reshaped by rapid technological change, persistent inequities, and the global pandemic. This chapter reviews global progress in research, policy, and practice, highlighting international strategic frameworks and the transformative impacts of COVID-19 and artificial intelligence (AI). Drawing on lessons from various interventions, this chapter concludes with an evidence-based vision for the future of STEM that prioritizes equity, sustainability, and systemic coherence across global learning ecosystems.

items.title: The Synergy Between Smart Grids and Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: This study explores the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) with smart grid systems to enhance renewable energy utilization and intelligent mobility. It highlights the transition from centralized power systems to decentralized, data-driven energy networks supported by IoT, big data, and advanced communication technologies. AI techniques such as machine learning and predictive analytics enable accurate demand forecasting, efficient energy management, and grid stability. The research also examines challenges in renewable integration, including intermittency and storage limitations, and presents AI-based solutions. Furthermore, it emphasizes the role of electric vehicles and vehicle-to-grid systems in achieving sustainable mobility, ultimately contributing to resilient, efficient, and environmentally friendly energy ecosystems.

items.title: The unbearable (and unsustainable) social impact of AI-generated “cultural monism” and the EU digital legislation
items.abstract: The increasing use of generative AI (genAI) across cultural and (re)creative sectors is indisputable in contemporary times. Within the EU, these systems are classified as “general-purpose AI” models (Recital 99 of the Artificial Intelligence Act – AI Act) and are expected to deliver a wide range of economic and societal benefits, as affirmed in Recital 105 of the Act. Yet, significant concerns have emerged regarding their potential impact on individuals, civil society, and democracy. In the cultural domain, genAI technologies are widely employed to generate outputs often perceived as original. However, scholarly debate has increasingly highlighted the risk that their widespread diffusion may lead to a form of cultural impoverishment – understood as the depletion of cultural pluralism and diversity of artistic expression resulting from the pervasive use of these systems and their underlying architectures, as well as, ultimately, an increasing standardization of the outputs of the algorithmic creative process. These systematic risks are not merely social or political but also carry significant legal implications. The potential effects of genAI on freedom of (artistic) expression and cultural pluralism may, in fact, infringe upon fundamental rights enshrined in international human rights charters. Yet, the role of legal scholarship in addressing such risks remains uncertain. A promising conceptual instrument for tackling this issue is the notion of systemic risk, recently introduced in two key pieces of EU digital legislation: the Digital Services Act (DSA) and the mentioned AI Act. This article examines the advantages and limitations of employing this concept to address the risk of cultural impoverishment. The analysis focuses primarily on the EU legal framework, with particular attention to the AI Act, while adopting a functional and comparative perspective, given that the principal challenges stem from US-based AI systems. It also situates the inquiry within the broader dynamics of the data economy, specifically the logic of knowledge capitalism. The article begins by exploring the potential impacts of genAI on cultural pluralism and artistic expression, assessing whether these may with time culminate in cultural impoverishment – or even a transition toward cultural monism, marked by the predominance, in all the cultural productions, of a single mainstream culture. It then analyses whether EU digital regulation is equipped to subsume such phenomena within the legal category of systemic risk.

items.title: The Unnoticed Freezes in the AI Era
items.abstract: In 2023, 18% of American adults said they had ever used ChatGPT. By early 2026, that number was 44%. AI adoption in the workplace has been even more remarkable. According to Microsoft's 2024 Work Trend Index, 75% of knowledge workers were already using AI at work, with nearly half having started within the preceding six months. We did not vote to hand over drafting, summarizing, fact-checking, and even thinking to these systems. There was no big decision. Just a free chatbot, a looming deadline, and a prompt that saved twenty minutes. Then another, and another... Regarding this serious issue, I was drawn to a new paper quietly posted on SSRN last September by Professor Vuong Quan Hoang. It gives this slow handover a name: the Correction Freeze Problem (CFP). His question is simple: can a system think it is fine while it is drifting away from reality, and stay that way not because it is lazy or lying, but because the very way it corrects itself makes staying blind the rational choice? The paper answers yes. In four different ways. And when any of those ways meets a world that rewards going along, the drift becomes a trap that is much harder to escape than it was to fall into. To grasp these insights, you don't need the math. Simply because you've lived it.

items.title: Theoretical Approaches to Understanding Sustained Physical Activity Behaviour
items.abstract: Physical activity is an essential requirement for a healthy life. And physical activity should be sustained for a long term. While there is a broad understanding and agreement that it is needed, per WHO report (2022) nearly 50% of Indian adult population does not do the required physical activity. There can be several reasons including COVID impact, Work from Home, Digital service revolution, etc. contributing to this inactivity. While these factors have a negative impact on physical activity, individual (intrinsic) factors do have an impact on behaviour of physical activity. There are several theories relating to human behaviour. This paper focusses on what theories can be leveraged to enable people to develop sustained physical activity behaviour. Two important psychological theories – Self Determination Theory (SDT) and Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB) are established theories in human behaviour domain. Components of these 2 theories and to what extent they relate to sustained physical activity behaviour are discussed in this paper. 25 participants of a physical activity program were interviewed. They were able to develop sustained physical activity. Researches in this area – SDT and TPB, empirical studies provide valuable insights into application of these theories to develop programs / interventions (by health care, government, fitness centres, families, peers, friends). Programs may need to be customized by agencies to enhance intrinsic motivation and behavioural intent that will have a positive impact on bringing the desirable change in individuals. Programs will need to apply other components of SDT and TPB as appropriate such that it contributes to the cause.

items.title: Think Faster, Argue Smarter: Combining GenAI-Assisted Prep and Human-Centered Rebuttals to Enhance Critical Thinking in Structured Debates
items.abstract: This experiential exercise adapts the traditional Oxford-style debate format to channel the pervasive student usage of Generative AI (GenAI) into a productive tension, inviting students to sharpen their critical reasoning, rhetorical discernment, and real-time argumentation skills. Students use GenAI to help them develop initial arguments and counterarguments, then engage in real-time rebuttals where they must think independently, respond to novel challenges, and adapt beyond their GenAI-prepared materials. This approach transforms GenAI from a potential crutch into a pedagogical catalyst that reveals the irreplaceable value of audience engagement, human judgment, critical thinking, and adaptive reasoning. The exercise forces students to scrutinize reasoning (both GenAI’s and their own) against standards of logic, clarity, and relevance, by confronting GenAI-assisted arguments and then dealing with spontaneous counterarguments. The exercise has been implemented in undergraduate strategic management and business ethics classes. It can also be valuable for higher-level courses and for other course subjects.

items.title: TILE: Bridging LLMs and Table Foundation Models for Tabular Learning with Strings
items.abstract: Real-world tables are often heterogeneous, combining numerical features with free-form string columns. Table foundation models (TFMs) excel on numerical tables but require strings to be encoded numerically, while large language models (LLMs) hold semantic knowledge but are not designed for tabular predictions. Most existing bridges use LLMs as plug-in encoders for cell strings, yet how to extract representations effectively for tabular learning remains underexplored. We show that the interface between LLMs and tables matter as much as the LLM itself. Applied cell-wise, larger LLMs do not give better features. With our interface, the same LLMs improve steadily with size. TILE (Table-Interfaced LLM Embeddings) combines four ingredients: row serialization to provide cross-column context, intermediate-layer extraction to avoid layers specialized for next-token prediction, columnar pooling to remove mean pooling's length bias, and by-pass features to route numbers and categories past the LLM. Paired with TFMs, TILE sets a new state of the art for tables with strings. Across 100 datasets, it beats the strongest baseline on 89% of splits, with gains across 7 LLMs and 10 tabular learners, and ranks first on the 108-dataset STRABLE benchmark.

items.title: TouchTwin: Human-AI Haptic Authoring for 3D-Scanned Tabletop Scenes through Language and Touch
items.abstract: Creating haptic experiences from real-world environments remains difficult: visual scans capture appearance but not material feel, while manual haptic authoring requires specialized expertise. We present TouchTwin, a human-AI approach that turns phone scans of tabletop scenes into editable haptic scenes. TouchTwin uses AI to propose material regions that users can experience and revise through language and spatial edits. A model trained on measured tool-surface interactions generates the haptic responses, allowing users to work with material descriptions rather than low-level signal parameters. In a study with N=12 participants and physical reference objects present, automatic drafts scored 4.0/7 for realism and 5.4/7 as useful starting points. After a median of 6.6 minutes of editing, realism increased to 5.6/7, while scoring the saved material layers against ground truth showed material-family accuracy improving from 52% to 92%. Participants also used the same workflow to author material feels without a physical reference.

items.title: Toward “Obesityomics”: Domain‐Specific Omics in Precision Obesity Medicine with a Brief AI Perspective
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Obesity's global rise has outpaced the effectiveness of "one-size-fits-all" prevention and treatment strategies. The promise of precision medicine lies in addressing the etiological and biological diversity of obesity and transforming it into actionable endotypes. OBJECTIVES: In a narrative review, we analyze "obesityomics," looking at the contributions each omics layer makes to understanding and managing obesity. The areas we evaluate are genomics (heritability, polygenic risk, and monogenic forms), epigenomics (development and environment imprinting), transcriptomics (tissue-specific programs of adipose, liver, muscle, and hypothalamus), proteomics (signaling networks and adipokines), metabolomics and lipidomics (fuel partitioning, lipotoxicity, and metabolic inflection points), and microbiome science (metabolites, host-microbe interactions, and microbial ecology). Our domain-by-domain (single-omics) approach demonstrates how disease taxonomy, causal pathways, and biomarkers can be refined and targeted therapeutically. DISCUSSION: We argue that "obesityomics" is a pragmatic approach to aligning omics modalities to the right questions at the right time, not a wholesale merger of datasets. Artificial intelligence (AI)-including machine learning and deep learning-should be used in conjunction with quality control, feature selection, modest data integration, and obesity intervention prediction. Among the key challenges in managing sensitive multilayer data are harmonization, standardization, reproducibility, equitable representation, and governance. The translation priorities include prospective studies related to patient-centered outcomes, biomarker panels that are clinic-ready, interoperability standards, and cost-effectiveness evaluations. CONCLUSION: The review maps concrete steps to assist people with obesity in making better choices by identifying what each omics domain excels at and introducing a brief AI perspective.

items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly explored in the Architecture, Engineering, and Construction (AEC) domain, yet their reliability in regulatory compliance remains uncertain. In this study, we evaluate the performance of LLMs on Hong Kong fire safety codes. In collaboration with domain experts, we create a localized benchmark dataset comprising both multiple-choice questions (MCQs) and open-ended questions (OEQs) to evaluate 12 widely used proprietary and open-source models. Our findings show that top-performing proprietary models achieve 80-90% accuracy on MCQs, whereas open-source models generally lag behind. However, on open-ended evaluation, expert human assessments reveal an accuracy range of only 50-70%, demonstrating that LLMs still have substantial room for improvement in specialized compliance tasks.

items.title: Towards Cost-Efficient Video Dataset Construction with Large Language Models
items.abstract: Research on video classification models has witnessed significant growth recently, accompanied by a significant increase in the demand for datasets to train such models. Existing video dataset curation approaches share a common bottleneck: candidate videos must be downloaded before any relevance judgment is made, which results in storage, time and annotation costs. In this work, we present a filtering step, using Large Language Models (LLMs) to pre-screen videos based on their metadata, before actually downloading these videos, thereby saving on these costs. We evaluate the LLMs against a strict human majority vote derived from four independent annotators and validate the reliability of the annotations through inter-annotator agreement analysis (Gwet's AC1). We compare the LLM pre-filter against two no-LLM baselines, namely two keyword heuristics. Via a Leave-One-Rater-Out (LOO) mechanism and an Add-One-Rater-In (AORI), we evaluate the performance of the LLMs as virtual annotators. Finally, we report cost comparisons relative to existing approaches. To ensure reproducability, we made our implementation available on github.

items.title: Towards Universal Calibration for In-Context Classification
items.abstract: In-Context Learning (ICL) has received a lot of interest recently due to its ability to improve classification accuracy for new tasks without having to fine-tune the model over these tasks. However, the impact of ICL on calibration has been far less studied. Recent work has shown that ICL can have a negative impact on calibration due to biased selection of in-context examples. The existing methods for improving ICL calibration require additional task and model-specific training, detracting from the no-fine-tuning convenience of ICL. In this work, we introduce CALIBFORMER, a universal ICL calibrator for classification tasks, that generalizes to new models and tasks without further fine-tuning on these tasks. Specifically, we design a transformer-based calibrator which uses the model predictions on in-context examples to predict a confidence score for the test input. We show that the calibrator trained on three models and ten tasks, is able to generalize/calibrate ICL predictions on several new tasks and four LLMs unseen during training. Even for frontier models like Gemini, CALIBFORMER is able to obtain over 50% reduction in calibration error.

items.title: TradeGraph: Learning Global Semiconductor Market Dynamics from International Trade Networks using Hybrid Graph Neural Networks
items.abstract: The global semiconductor industry has become a strategic pillar of the digital economy and mainly supports the artificial intelligence technology, cloud computing, advanced manufacturing, and modern electronic devices. Forecasting international semiconductor trade flows is therefore essential for governments, researchers, and policymakers. In this paper, we propose TradeGraph, a hybrid Graph Neural Network (GNN) architecture that combines Graph Attention Networks (GAT), Graph Convolutional Networks (GCN) and GraphSAGE through an adaptive gated fusion mechanism for bilateral trade flow prediction. This research used the BACI international trade database. First, we analyze the structural evolution of the global semiconductor trade network and identify its major trading communities. Then, we develop a hybrid GNN model that we compare with three baseline GNN architectures under a temporal train-validation-test split, to predict the semiconductor trade flow. Experimental results demonstrate that TradeGraph achieves the best predictive performance and exhibits lower variability across multiple independent runs. Our results reveal that the global semiconductor market is characterized by a limited number of major trade blocs and suggest an increasing importance of Asian economies in the global semiconductor trade network over the study period. These findings demonstrate the potential of hybrid Graph Neural Networks for analyzing and forecasting complex international trade networks.

A systematic literature review (SLR) following PRISMA 2020 was applied to journal articles from Google Scholar, Garuda, Neliti, and Scopus. The matrix evolves through administrative, strategy-linked, and digitally adaptive stages. Digital transformation shifts competency demands toward digital, data, and behavioral skills, while technologies such as enterprise systems and artificial intelligence bring efficiency but also the risk of dehumanization. The study proposes an integrative framework and a research agenda.

items.title: Transforming Agriculture through Emerging Technologies for Sustainable Productivity
items.abstract: The convergence of robotics and precision agriculture (PA) marks a transformative shift in modern farming practices aimed at enhancing productivity and ensuring long-term sustainability. This chapter explores the integration of advanced robotic systems into agricultural operations to address critical challenges such as labor shortages, resource inefficiency, and environmental degradation. It provides an in-depth analysis of various robotic applications, ranging from autonomous tractors, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) (drones), and robotic arms to artificial intelligence (AI)-driven monitoring systems that contribute to site-specific crop management, precision irrigation, pesticide application, and harvesting. The chapter emphasizes how robotics, when combined with sensor technologies, data analytics, and machine learning (ML), enables real-time decision-making and optimized farm management. Furthermore, it discusses the socio-economic and environmental benefits of adopting robotic solutions, along with the barriers to implementation and future research directions. By offering a comprehensive overview, this chapter aims to serve as a foundational reference for researchers, practitioners, and policymakers committed to the advancement of sustainable and high-efficiency agriculture through robotics.

items.title: Transforming Mathematics Teacher Education Through Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation: Extent of Utilization, Challenges, and Strategies in Colleges of Education, Gombe State
items.abstract: This study investigated the extent of utilization, challenges, and strategies for transforming mathematics teacher education through artificial intelligence (AI) and digital innovation in Colleges of Education in Gombe State, Nigeria. Anchored on the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework, the study adopted a descriptive survey design involving 75 stakeholders (21 administrators and 54 mathematics lecturers) drawn by census sampling from Colleges of Education in Gombe State. Data were collected using a validated 30-item questionnaire (Cronbach alpha = 0.84) and analysed using mean, standard deviation, and independent-samples t-test at the 0.05 level of significance. Findings revealed that AI and digital tools are utilized to a low extent overall in mathematics teacher education (cumulative mean = 2.70), with only dynamic geometry software and mobile learning applications utilized to a high extent. Ten challenges were affirmed as significant, most notably inadequate ICT infrastructure, high cost of digital devices and data, and lack of institutional policy on AI use (cumulative mean = 4.06), while resistance to change and data-privacy concerns were not strongly endorsed as major challenges. Nine strategies were identified as needed to enhance AI and digital integration, most notably reliable electricity and internet infrastructure and regular capacity-building training for lecturers (cumulative mean = 4.05). The t-test results showed no statistically significant difference between administrators' and lecturers' perceptions across extent of utilization (t = 1.05, p = 0.30), challenges (t = 0.55, p = 0.58), and strategies (t = 0.60, p = 0.55). The study concludes that despite low current utilization, stakeholders strongly endorse both the barriers and the pathways toward meaningful AI-driven transformation of mathematics teacher education, and recommends deliberate infrastructural investment and sustained capacity building as priority interventions.

items.title: Translation indeterminacy and the distributional fallacy
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are commonly associated with the distributional hypothesis, according to which (1) semantic meaning is grounded in distributional patterns of linguistic context, and (2) knowledge of cross-linguistic distributional correspondences allows for successful translation. This paper rejects the first claim as a causal inversion: linguistic distributions reflect patterns arising from meaning-making practices rather than constituting their source. At the same time, it accepts the second claim, arguing that translation -human or machine - can succeed without requiring access to meaning or reference. Knowledge of interlingual distributional correspondence and their inferential organization may be sufficient for translation. The paper develops an ecological-enactivist perspective, according to which reference and meaning are grounded in agent-environment interaction and stabilized through action-grounded concepts, forms of world-involving cognition that current LLMs do not possess.

items.title: Translators’ Gains and Pains in the Era of Generative Artificial Intelligence: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: This study aimed to provide a comprehensive systematic review of research published in peer-reviewed scientific journals in Arabic and English between 2022 and 2026 that investigated the impact of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools, such as ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Copilot, and others, on translation and translation education among professional translators, translation students, and faculty members. The study used the PRISMA 2020 framework for systematic search, screening, and documentation, and employed a thematic analysis approach based on the model developed by Braun and Clarke. After applying the inclusion and exclusion criteria to 24 initial records, the final analysis included 18 studies. The findings revealed that the most significant benefits of using generative AI tools included improved efficiency and productivity, reduced time to complete translation tasks, support for post-editing processes, improved certain translation quality indicators, and the promotion of self-directed learning and the development of professional competencies among translators and students. At the same time, the results identified several challenges, most notably terminological accuracy issues, difficulties handling cultural and idiomatic expressions and local dialects, risks associated with overreliance on intelligent systems, and ethical concerns involving privacy, transparency, and professional accountability. The review also showed that the impact of generative AI varies by text type, specialized domain, and the assessment tools used. In addition, it highlighted limited evidence available concerning the Arabic language, particularly in areas such as legal translation, idiomatic expressions, and local dialects. This study contributes an interpretive framework based on the concept of “Gains and Pains” to explain generative AI’s dual impact on translation and translation education. The findings conclude that generative AI does not fully replace human translators; rather, it serves as a supportive tool that reshapes translators’ professional roles toward reviewing, verifying, and evaluating outputs. Accordingly, the study recommends integrating generative AI tools into translator training programs within clear pedagogical and ethical frameworks. They should also include post-editing, critical thinking, and output-verification skills, and support further specialized applied research in the Arab context.

items.title: Transparent Information Flow Modeling for Role-Aware AI Act Assessment
items.abstract: The European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act introduces a structured framework for governing high-risk AI systems, emphasizing transparency, risk management, and role-specific accountability. However, current assessment practices often rely on monolithic system views or disconnected checklists, limiting their ability to capture the socio-technical complexity of real-world deployments. We explore the use of the Information Flow Methodology (IFM), a modeling-based approach to AI Act compliance assessment. IFM represents decision systems -- whether algorithmic, human, or hybrid -- as networks of information sites and transformation channels, enabling structured analysis of how information, decisions, and responsibilities flow across organizational and technical boundaries. We apply IFM in a real-world case involving a recruitment support tool used by a public-sector organization, evaluating both the Provider's system and the Deployer's recruitment process. Our results demonstrate that IFM can serve as a scaffold to bridge both component-based and holistic perspectives, and how technical systems are situated within socio-technical contexts. In doing so, IFM supports transparency, identifies risk pathways, and enables alignment analysis between intended and actual use. We argue that such modeling provides a foundational tool for effective, context-sensitive AI governance and accountability -- offering capabilities beyond conventional checklist-based assessments.

items.title: TRAP: Tree-Guided Reinforcement-Augmented Probing for Automated LLM Jailbreaking
items.abstract: Aligned large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak prompts that circumvent their safety guardrails, making the identification of these vulnerabilities important for understanding and mitigating model weaknesses. Existing automated jailbreak methods explore prompt candidates or reuse attack experience, but generally do not learn over a persistent hierarchy that connects related jailbreak strategies, such as role-play, encoding, and obfuscation. This leaves the relationships among reusable strategies underused in guiding adaptive attack selection. We present Tree-Guided Reinforcement-Augmented Probing (TRAP), a hierarchical framework for automated jailbreak strategy discovery that requires only black-box access to the target LLM. TRAP organizes established jailbreak methods and successful attack templates into a semantic strategy tree, connecting broad attack approaches to concrete, reusable strategies. A reinforcement-learning policy based on a tree-structured gradient bandit explores this tree and uses evaluator feedback to update strategy preferences along each selected path. The policy retains these preferences across attack objectives, allowing experience from earlier attempts to guide subsequent strategy selection. Retrieval-augmented prompt construction translates the selected strategy into an attack for the current objective using relevant successful examples. Experiments on AdvBench across seven aligned LLMs show that TRAP outperforms its counterparts on six models under the reported method settings and the common primary evaluator, achieving attack success rates of 45.6% to 97.9% on these models. These findings support hierarchical strategy learning as an effective approach to discovering jailbreak vulnerabilities in aligned LLMs.

items.title: TriAlign UDA for hybrid domain adaptation of frozen histopathology foundation model representations
items.abstract: Foundation models produce strong patch-level representations in histopathological image analysis; however, domain shifts across different centers, staining protocols, and scanner conditions can limit the direct generalizability of these representations. In this study, a hybrid feature-level unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) framework called TriAlign-UDA, which operates on frozen histopathology foundation model representations, is proposed. TriAlign-UDA aims to reduce the mismatch between the labeled source domain and the completely unlabeled target domain without requiring encoder fine-tuning. The method combines statistical alignment, prototype-based semantic preservation, and adversarial adaptation components within a common learning framework based on a bottleneck residual adapter. In the experiments, NCT-CRC-HE-100K was used as the labeled source domain, TCGA-COAD/READ as the unlabeled target domain, and CRC-VAL-HE-7K as the independent external evaluation dataset. In the results obtained over five different seeds, TriAlign-UDA reached the highest mean accuracy of 0.9669 ± 0.0050, balanced accuracy of 0.9560 ± 0.0063, and Macro-F1 of 0.9515 ± 0.0067 on CRC-VAL-HE-7K among the evaluated methods, including the recent EUDA and PLADA-f baselines. DANN and EUDA produced closely competitive results; however, the differences between TriAlign-UDA and DANN, EUDA, or PLADA-f did not reach statistical significance. These findings indicate that frozen-feature UDA should be evaluated not only through individual alignment objectives but also through independent external generalization performance.

items.title: TrustGuard: A Risk-Aware Human Oversight Framework for Safe Autonomous AI Agents
items.abstract: Autonomous AI agents can perform increasingly consequential actions on behalf of users, creating a need for human oversight that is proportional to the potential risk of each action. This paper presents TrustGuard, a lightweight and interpretable risk-aware human oversight framework for AI agents. TrustGuard automatically evaluates proposed actions using five factors: privacy risk, financial risk, data modification risk, irreversibility risk, and external impact. Each factor is scored from zero to five, producing a total score from zero to twenty-five. Based on the score, actions are classified as Low, Medium, or High Risk and mapped to autonomous execution, user confirmation, or human approval. A prototype was implemented using Python and Streamlit to demonstrate the framework. The rule-based analyzer was calibrated using 120 development scenarios and subsequently evaluated on a held-out pilot set of 30 new scenarios. TrustGuard correctly classified 27 of the 30 test scenarios, achieving 90 percent accuracy. The results demonstrate the potential of transparent risk-based oversight while also identifying limitations in detecting some security-sensitive and privacy-sensitive actions.

items.title: Tumor antigens across cancer progression: from immune recognition and selection to precision cancer immunotherapy
items.abstract: Tumor antigens provide the molecular interface between malignant transformation and host immunity, but their biological significance is determined by more than their molecular existence. Antigen clonality, abundance, processing, human leukocyte antigen (HLA) presentation, dendritic-cell function, T-cell recognition, spatial immune organization, and the surrounding tumor microenvironment (TME) collectively determine whether an antigen becomes immunologically visible and therapeutically actionable. Across cancer progression, tumor-cell antigenic states and the TME undergo reciprocal selection: immune pressure can eliminate highly visible clones while favoring antigen-loss variants, HLA defects, immune exclusion, suppressive myeloid and stromal states, and treatment-resistant populations. Recent single-cell, spatial and three-dimensional imaging, as well as immunopeptidomic studies show that this evolution is heterogeneous across tumor regions and anatomical compartments rather than a uniform linear process. This review therefore advances an antigen-TME co-evolution framework linking primary tumors, lymphatic and nodal immune compartments, systemic dissemination, distant metastatic niches, therapy, minimal residual disease, and recurrence. It critically evaluates the strengths and limitations of the classical immunoediting model; compares melanoma, breast, colorectal, lung, prostate, sarcoma, and virus-associated cancers according to antigen source, clonality, presentation competence, immune architecture, and dominant therapeutic bottleneck; and examines clinical translation through checkpoint blockade, cellular therapy, vaccines, antibodies, antibody-drug conjugates, immunopeptidomics, and computational antigen prediction. Particular attention is given to the gap between predicted peptide binding and verified presentation or immunogenicity, the need for longitudinal rather than single-biopsy profiling, and the requirement for prospective validation of artificial-intelligence models. The central conclusion is that tumor antigens become clinically meaningful only when antigenic state and microenvironmental context are assessed together, providing a more rigorous foundation for precision cancer immunotherapy.

items.title: Uncovering Robustness Weaknesses in LLM Agents via Persona Evolution with Task-Integrity Constraints
items.abstract: Interactive-agent evaluations commonly rely on standardized LLM-based user simulators that exhibit broadly cooperative behavior, potentially overlooking failures that arise under diverse but realistic user interactions. This can lead to overly optimistic estimates of agent robustness and provide limited failure signals for training agents that generalize across users. Existing approaches largely rely on predefined user behaviors, which may miss agent- or domain-specific weaknesses, while failure-oriented search can reduce task success by invalidating the underlying task rather than exposing genuine robustness failures. To fill this gap, we introduce TIPER, a task-integrity-preserving persona evolution method that automatically discovers agent-specific user policies exposing robustness weaknesses while keeping the underlying task valid and solvable. TIPER evolves persistent user personas through reflection-guided behavioral mutations and task-wise Pareto selection under a task-integrity constraint. Across four interactive-agent benchmarks, TIPER yields lower held-out avg@3 scores in all 12 GPT-5.4 settings, with observed reductions of 5.8 to 33.7 percentage points, and in all 28 agent-domain pairs spanning seven agents, with a median observed reduction of 22.9 points. Further analysis yields a behavior-to-failure taxonomy that connects discovered user behaviors to recurring agent failure modes. Together, these results show that TIPER enables more diagnostic robustness evaluation of interactive agents and provides informative failure analysis for future agent robustness improvement. Code repository: https://github.com/UCSB-NLP-Chang/TIPER.

items.title: Universities as Engines of AI Sovereignty
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping governance and economic systems worldwide, yet many countries in the Global South remain dependent on technologies, infrastructures, and governance models produced elsewhere. This dependency reflects deeper patterns of digital colonialism, including data extraction, reliance on foreign cloud systems, and limited capacity to shape AI on local terms. Grounded in African empirical evidence with broader application across the Global South, this paper argues that universities are critical but overlooked institutions in efforts to strengthen AI sovereignty. While governments, firms, and civil society face persistent capability gaps, universities hold mandates that position them to build research capacity, cultivate technical and governance expertise, and coordinate innovation ecosystems. Drawing on political economy and higher education scholarship, the paper develops the Capability–Alignment–Impact (CAI) Framework to explain how universities can contribute to autonomous AI development through three pathways: strengthening foundational knowledge; improving coordination across government, industry, and civil society; and translating expertise into societal impact. The paper concludes by outlining practical implications for policymakers, development agencies, and university leaders seeking to support sovereign AI ecosystems in the Global South.
